units.text: The Exceptionally High Dielectric Constant of Doped Organic Semiconductors
Introduction

The dielectric constant (ɛ r ) is a key property of a semiconductor as it characterizes the ability to screen charge.[3][4] Efforts to enhance ɛ r of organic semiconductors have focused on synthetic approaches, [5][6][7] such as side-chain DOI: 10.1002/aelm.202400413[10] A significant increased ɛ r has been reported in various conjugated polymers, [11,12] small molecules, [13,14] and fullerene derivatives with polar side chains. [6,10,15]By introducing polar side-chain groups, dipoles can reorient in response to an electric field, thereby modulating ɛ r while maintaining the core structure of the material. [6]Among such polar side chains, ethylene glycol chains are particularly suitable due to their flexibility facilitating charge transfer in the solid state without morphological hindrance. [16][26] The doping process involves the introduction of electron donors or acceptors into the host matrix and chemically generating additional free charge carriers, thus altering the charge carrier density and conductivity.However, the ionized dopants and free charge carriers still experience Coulomb attraction, which limits the generation of free charges and the conductivity as argued by Arkhipov. [27,28]The dielectric constant of doped organic semiconductors is thus of great importance as it directly impacts the doping process.

In a recent paper, we have put forward that there exists equally strong Coulomb repulsion among free charge carriers, in addition to the Coulomb attraction from charge-counterion pairs. [29]hrough kinetic Monte Carlo simulations and the experimental results involving the combined dependence of electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient on carrier density, we have demonstrated that carrier-carrier repelling forces can be significantly strong to dominate over the intrinsic energetic disorder and consequently impose a constraint on charge transport. [29]Similarly, through kMC simulations, Liu et al. have demonstrated that charge transport can be affected by carrier-carrier interactions in undoped organic semiconductors. [30]Additionally, Lungwitz et al. used photoemission spectroscopy to characterize the onsite Coulomb interactions between electrons (Hubbard U) in an n-doped conjugated polymer.This provides further evidence for the existence of carrier-carrier Coulomb interactions. [31]These findings demonstrate the further importance of dielectric properties as they also dictate the interactions among charge carriers.D'Avino et al. recently studied the effect of collective screening in doped organic semiconductors. [32]Briefly, this collective effect reduces the barrier to the generation of free carriers from dopants by screening the Coulomb interaction.As a result, the relative dielectric constant sharply increases upon doping, leading to a dielectric catastrophe. [32]It is not unreasonable to assume that the polarizability of the charge transfer states depends on specific properties such as ionization potential, but the collective response of charge carriers should be more general.Subsequently, Koch et al. experimentally proved that the dielectric constant of lightly p-doped polymer increases from ≈3.0 (pristine) to 4.9 (lightly doped). [33]However, the dielectric catastrophe responsible for the significant enhancement of ɛ r at higher doping levels remains to be explored.

In this contribution, we utilize metal-insulator-semiconductor (MIS) devices to conduct a series of dielectric constant measurements based on poly[[N,N-bis(2-octyl dodecyl)-naphthalene-1,4,5,8-bis (dicarboximide)-2,6-diyl]-alt-5,5′-(2,2′-bithio-phene)] (N2200) and regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT) as n-and p-type organic semiconductors respectively, under various doping concentrations.MIS diodes are commonly used to measure the carrier density in doped organic semiconductors.Here, we show that MIS diodes can also be used to measure the dielectric constant.This includes the high-doping regime which is typically difficult to assess due to the corresponding high electrical conductivities.Specifically, we focus on analyzing the weak inversion region of the MIS devices at a specific frequency, as the capacitance in this region is approximately equal to the capacitance of the semiconductor layer.Our results demonstrate that the dielectric constant shows a strong increase upon doping in both n-type and p-type doped organic materials, spanning a range from ≈3.0 to 15.0, confirming the existence of a dielectric catastrophe as predicted by D'Avino. [32]These observations provide further evidence to substantiate the significant influence of molecular doping on the dielectric constant, and underscore the importance of characterizing the dielectric properties of doped organic semiconductors.
Materials and Device Fabrication

As illustrated in Figure 1, P3HT is presented as a p-type semiconductor, with 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) employed as its corresponding dopant.N2200 emerges as the predominant n-type organic semiconductor, wherein 4-(2,3-dihydro-1,3-dimethyl-1H-benzimidazol-2-yl)-N,N-dimethylbenzenamine (NDMBI) acting as the dopant.

The MIS device is the basic apparatus for investigating interface charging and electrical properties, such as charge carrier mobility. [34]and carrier density. [2,35,36]It has widespread application in organic semiconductor structures such as capacitors, [37] light-emitting diodes, [38] and organic thermoelectric devices. [20,36]n this current study, we use a configuration comprising an indium tin oxide (ITO)/insulator/semiconductor layer/aluminum (Al) setup.

For insulator layer preparation, 251 mg poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) (PVDF-HFP) was dissolved  ) was added to the solution and stirred at 55 °C until 1 h before spin-coating. [3]Ion gel solution was spin-coated on UV-ozone treated clean ITO substrates, followed by annealing at 130 °C for 4 h to obtain a solidified layer, the thickness is ≈150-300 nm. [3]he ITO layer functions as the bottom electrode, while the [EMIM][TFSI]/PVDF-HFP layer serves as the insulator.

The organic semiconductor layers were prepared by spincoating doped organic semiconductor solutions on top of insulators to ensure a uniform and smooth surface.The doped solution was prepared with chloroform solutions (5 mg ml −1 for N2200 and 10 mg ml −1 for P3HT) mixed with different amounts of dopant chloroform solutions (10 mg ml −1 for NDMBI and 1 mg ml −1 for F4TCNQ), the doping concentrations here are the mole ratio of dopant per molecule.

The Al electrode was evaporated in the following step, with a thickness of 100 nm.After the top electrode, the devices containing doped N2200 were annealed in a hotplate at 120 °C for 1 h and cooled to room temperature for the following measurements.Additional details regarding the device can be found in the supplementary information.
Results and Discussion

The MIS device shows a distinctive behavior as a function of applied voltage.Figure 2 shows three distinct colored regimes, corresponding to three capacitance (C p )-bottom voltage (V) characteristics that vary with the bias voltage.The purple area in Figure 2b,c corresponds to the strong accumulation region.The majority carriers in this region within the semiconductor layer accumulate at the semiconductor interface under the influence of the bias voltage.As the bias voltage varies, charge carriers diffuse from the interface to the semiconductor bulk, forming the depletion region (presented in blue in Figure 2).The carrier density can be obtained through the Mott-Schottky formula. In this study, we employ Equation ( 4) to evaluate the dielectric constant of doped organic semiconductor layers.

For the correct use of the MIS diode measurements, it is important to select the right frequency range.The response of the ion gel is relatively slow (as it is ionic in nature), with the dielectric constant of the ion gel falling off at frequencies > 1 kHz (see Figure S1a, Supporting Information).The selection of a frequency value of 10 Hz is based on the logic that C i remains valid during the accumulation bias at this frequency, and any inversion features arising from the charging/discharging dynamics can be considered negligible. [2]The injected charges during accumulation can adequately respond up to the point of capacitance dispersion. [34]This cut-off frequency is determined from the frequency response of the sample measured at various doping concentrations.Our results demonstrate the absence of capacitance dispersion at a frequency of ≈10 Hz, as shown in Figure S1b,c (Supporting Information).

We analyzed the dielectric constant of the P3HT system.Figure 3a represents the C p d sc /ɛ 0 value derived from the measured capacitance using Equation ( 4).The gray regime (3.6 to  5.2 V) corresponds to the weak inversion region in Figure 2b, and the dielectric constant is the average extracted from the C p d sc /ɛ 0 values within this regime.The ɛ r values with the standard deviations as the error from a minimum of five samples are listed in Table 1.calculated ɛ r increases from 2.9 in pristine P3HT to 4.0 for the p-doped P3HT with the P3HT:F4TCNQ ration of 1000:1, consistent with findings from a previous study. [1,33]esides analyzing ɛ r of the p-doped organic semiconductor, we applied this methodology to the n-doped organic semiconductor (NDMBI-doped N2200).Figure 3b depicts the C p d sc /ɛ 0 value of the measured capacitance, where the dielectric constant is extracted in the voltage range from -2.4 to -0.7 V (gray regime).Average ɛ r values and standard deviations from six samples are summarized in Table 2.The capacitance of pristine N2200 yields an ɛ r of ≈3.0, consistent with the literature. [1]The ɛ r is enhanced within the region of weak inversion with the gradual increase in the dopant concentration, as shown in Figure 3b.

Figure 4 shows the correlation between the dielectric constant and doping concentration, represented as red dots and dash, respectively.The dielectric constant considerably increases from 2.9 in case of the pristine P3HT to 11.4 in case of the F4TCNQdoped P3HT film with a ratio of P3HT:F4TCNQ of 20:1.The dielectric constant of NDMBI-doped N2200 films is in the range of 3.0-14.5 with the addition of NDMBI to pristine N2200, reaching a doping ratio of N2200:NDMBI of 9:1.

The density of free carriers can also be obtained from MIS measurements, as shown in Equation ( 1).In the literature, it is common to use the pristine value of ɛ r in Equation ( 1). [2,20,36]In order to facilitate a comparison with the literature, we took the same approach (i.e.ɛ r = 3.0) in order to obtain the carrier densities shown in Figure 4.In Figure 4, we show the relation between the doping concentration, the dielectric constant and the extracted carrier density assuming ɛ r = 3.0.One can also take the dependence of the dielectric constant on the doping level into account in Equation ( 1) and obtain the data as shown in Figure S3 and Table S1 (Supporting Information).Although the adoption of the extracted ɛ r instead of 3.0 reduces the carrier density range, the nonlinear correlation between the dielectric constant and carrier density is evident.These experimental results confirm the theoretical calculations reported by D'Avino et al., [32] which predict the occurrence of a dielectric catastrophe induced by the introduction of dopants.

It should be noted that the nanoscale interactions between charges in doped films are not screened by the dielectric constant that we report here (Figure 4), as that would be a form of double counting as the mobile charges contribute to the measured dielectric constant.Our previous work has shown that such mobile charge carriers shield dopants very effectively. [29]This behavior is consistent with the collective screen phenomenon reported by D'Avino and our experiments.Both cases suggest that charges still interact via Coulomb interaction, otherwise, no collective behavior exists.Although the screening of charges increases free carrier yield, this collective behavior can decrease the conductivity due to the domination of carrier-carrier interactions under high carrier densities.
Conclusion

In summary, we used MIS diodes to measure the dielectric constant of doped organic semiconductors.This versatile method can be applied to both n-and p-doped organic materials and is not constrained by specific doping concentrations owing to the charge shielding effect of the insulator layer.We measured the dielectric constant of the doped P3HT and N2200 across a broad range of doping concentrations up to 5.0 mol% and 11.1 mol%, respectively.Our study revealed a distinct nonlinear increase of ɛ r from ≈3.0 to 15.0, resembling the phenomenon of dielectric catastrophe.These empirical observations align with recent theoretical investigations of the influence of molecular doping on ɛ r and reiterate the existence of Coulomb interaction among charge carriers in doped organic semiconductors.
